clinicalPearls: An aggressive malignant germ-cell tumour of children and young women that characteristically secretes alpha-fetoprotein
Typically presents with a rapidly growing pelvic or abdominal mass and pain, sometimes with acute symptoms from torsion or rupture
Serum AFP is an invaluable tumour marker for diagnosis, monitoring treatment response, and detecting recurrence
The classic histological hallmark is the Schiller-Duval body, a glomeruloid structure with a central vessel, though many architectural patterns exist
Almost always unilateral, which supports fertility-sparing surgery in appropriately selected young patients
Highly chemosensitive, so platinum-based germ-cell chemotherapy is central to management and has transformed outcomes
May occur as part of a mixed germ-cell tumour, so thorough sampling and correlation with other markers are important
reference.pathophysiology: Ovarian yolk sac tumour is a malignant germ-cell neoplasm that differentiates towards extra-embryonic yolk sac and allantoic structures, recapitulating the endodermal sinus of the developing embryo. This differentiation explains the production of alpha-fetoprotein, a normal yolk sac product, which serves as a specific serum marker. Histologically the tumour displays diverse patterns, the most recognisable being the Schiller-Duval body, a papillary tuft with a central capillary that resembles a primitive glomerulus, together with intracellular and extracellular hyaline globules. The tumour grows rapidly and disseminates readily within the abdomen, but its germ-cell lineage confers marked sensitivity to chemotherapy, which underpins the possibility of cure even in advanced disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other malignant germ-cell tumours (dysgerminoma, immature teratoma, embryonal carcinoma)
Clear cell carcinoma of the ovary
Epithelial ovarian carcinoma in a young woman
additionalInvestigations: Serum AFP as the principal tumour marker, with beta-hCG and LDH to assess for a mixed germ-cell component
Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound of the mass
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for staging
Histology with immunohistochemistry (e.g. AFP, glypican-3, SALL4)
Baseline assessment of the contralateral ovary and uterus for fertility planning
Renal and general organ function assessment before chemotherapy
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging pelvic mass with markedly raised AFP in a child or young woman
Acute abdomen from torsion or rupture of the tumour
Evidence of intra-abdominal dissemination or rising markers during follow-up
Features suggesting a mixed germ-cell tumour requiring broader treatment
reference.prognosis: Historically dismal but now substantially improved by platinum-based chemotherapy; early-stage disease has a high cure rate, and even advanced tumours can be cured, with AFP trends guiding treatment.
pitfalls: Delaying diagnosis of a rapidly growing ovarian mass in a young patient
Not measuring AFP, thereby losing a key diagnostic and monitoring tool
Failing to recognise a mixed germ-cell component that alters management
Choosing overly radical surgery when fertility-sparing treatment is appropriate
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with preservation of the uterus and contralateral ovary is the standard surgical approach, given the near-universal unilaterality of this tumour
Fertility-sparing surgery is appropriate even in the presence of metastatic disease, since this tumour class is exquisitely chemosensitive
Surgical staging of the abdomen and pelvis informs disease extent but does not override the need for adjuvant chemotherapy in this histology

Adjuvant combination chemotherapy with a platinum agent plus etoposide and bleomycin follows surgery for essentially all patients, since yolk sac tumour does not fall under the stage IA dysgerminoma or low-grade immature teratoma exceptions that allow observation alone

Observation after complete resection of a strictly confined stage IA tumour is sometimes considered at select low-volume centres with close marker and imaging follow-up, but this is a general oncology practice rather than a carve-out for this histology and should be approached cautiously
Advanced, recurrent, or metastatic disease is still treated with curative intent given the marked chemosensitivity of this tumour class
The treatment framework is extrapolated from the more extensively studied testicular germ cell tumour experience
Radiotherapy is not part of standard management for this histology
Serum alpha-fetoprotein is the key tumour marker and should be followed serially during and after treatment to assess response and detect recurrence
Long-term surveillance should attend to fertility and reproductive outcomes, since return of normal menstrual function is the rule and successful pregnancies are commonly documented in survivors
Management should involve a gynaecologic oncology and germ cell tumour multidisciplinary team from diagnosis given the rarity, young patient population, and fertility considerations
Suspicion of a mixed germ cell tumour component, rising markers on surveillance, or recurrent disease should prompt prompt referral back to the multidisciplinary team
